paragraphs: If a person had before him various kinds of fruit, and among them are fruits of the seven species for which the Land of Israel is praised, the fruits for which the Land of Israel is praised take precedence over other tree fruits. And not only that, but even among the fruits for which the Land of Israel is praised themselves, one takes precedence over another according to the order in which Scripture lists them in the verse (Deuteronomy 8:8): "A land of wheat and barley, vines and figs and pomegranates, a land of olive oil and honey" — five kinds of fruit are mentioned here, for the "honey" mentioned here is dates. This is the order of their precedence, one after another: grapes, whether fresh or dried, precede figs, and all the more so pomegranates; and figs precede pomegranates. But dates precede grapes, because dates are mentioned second in relation to the latter "land," while grapes are mentioned third in relation to the first "land." And the olive precedes dates, and also precedes grapes, because the olive is first in relation to the latter "land." But it does not precede wine, even though it is first in relation to the latter "land," because the importance of wine is very great, and also its blessing is more distinctly defined, for one recites "borei peri hagafen" only over wine — and any blessing fixed specifically for a particular species contains more praise of the Holy One, blessed be He, for it shows His particular providence in greater detail.

clarification.explanation: Among the kinds of fruit before a person — fruits of the seven species for which the Land of Israel is praised take precedence over other tree fruits, and even among themselves there is an order of precedence following the order of the verse "a land of wheat and barley, vines and figs and pomegranates, a land of olive oil and honey" (honey = dates): grapes precede figs and all the more so pomegranates; figs precede pomegranates; dates precede grapes (because dates are mentioned second in relation to the second "land," while grapes are mentioned third in relation to the first "land"); the olive precedes dates and grapes (being first in relation to the second "land"), but does not precede wine (despite being first in relation to the second "land") because of the special importance of wine and its distinctly defined blessing ("borei peri hagafen" specifically for wine) — and this teaches a general principle: any blessing fixed specifically for a particular species (rather than a general blessing that applies to many species) contains greater praise of the Holy One, blessed be He, since it shows His particular providence over each and every thing.
takeaways: Order of precedence in blessing: the seven species before other fruits; and among the five fruit kinds themselves the order is: olive first, then dates, then grapes, then figs, and last pomegranates — not simply in the order mentioned in the verse.
Wine precedes the olive despite the order of the verse, because of its special importance and its own distinct blessing.

A blessing fixed specifically for a particular species (such as "borei peri hagafen" specifically for wine) praises God more, because it expresses His particular providence over each individual thing.

paragraphs: Some say that if there is a fruit that is not of the seven species but is more beloved to him, he gives it precedence even over a fruit of the seven species. However, the plain ruling of Maran, whose rulings we have accepted, is not so, and the widespread custom among us is to give precedence to a fruit of the seven species over everything, following the plain ruling of Maran. Nevertheless, a fruit of the seven species does not take precedence over other fruits unless its ripening is complete; therefore, pickled olives, which are very small and appear to the eye not yet fully ripened, do not take precedence.

clarification.explanation: Some hold that a fruit especially beloved (even if not of the seven species) precedes the seven species, but the custom (and Maran's ruling) is to always give precedence to the seven species. The seven species take precedence only after their ripening is complete — therefore small pickled olives that appear not yet fully ripened do not take precedence.
takeaways: The seven species always take precedence (despite personal preference for another fruit), but only if their ripening is complete.

paragraphs: One should be careful to recite the blessing over the cleanest and most beautiful fruit, because of "This is my God and I will beautify Him" (Exodus 15:2), and should give precedence to "borei peri ha'etz" over "borei peri ha'adamah," and likewise give precedence to "borei peri ha'adamah" over the blessing of "shehakol." Only if he has before him kinds of sweets made of cane sugar, which comes from canes that are a kind of tree, over which one recites "shehakol" out of doubt due to a dispute regarding blessings, and he also has before him a fruit of a tree that certainly requires "ha'etz" — in that case he gives precedence to reciting the blessing over the cane sweet before the tree fruit, as we wrote regarding the previous Shabbat (paragraph 16) in the name of Rabbi Eliyah Rabbah. But sugar made from a ground fruit called "spandar" (beet) he should not give precedence over tree fruit, but he should give it precedence over ground fruit because of the aforementioned doubt regarding blessings. And if he has before him a kind of sweet called "man sama" ("from heaven" — a sweetener made from the dew found on the leaves of trees), which is from the dew of heaven, then its blessing is "shehakol" as a matter of law and not because of doubt; and likewise truffles and the like, whose blessing is "shehakol" as a matter of law, should be blessed over after tree or ground produce.

clarification.explanation: One should bless over the cleanest and most beautiful fruit ("this is my God and I will beautify Him"). Order of blessings: "borei peri ha'etz" before "borei peri ha'adamah," and this before "shehakol." But if he has before him cane sugar (blessed "shehakol" out of doubt) and a certain tree fruit — he gives precedence to blessing over the sugar, because this is preferable in terms of the order of doubts; whereas sugar from beet (a ground produce) — he gives it precedence only over ground produce. "Man sama" (dew sweetener) and truffles — their blessing is "shehakol" as a matter of law (not out of doubt), and one blesses over them after tree or ground produce.
takeaways: Order of blessings: tree → ground → shehakol.
Sugar under doubt (from cane) precedes a certain tree fruit in blessing, for reasons of the order of doubts.

paragraphs: All the laws of precedence that we have written apply only where both kinds are before him and he wishes to eat from both; but if both are not before him, one does not tell him to wait until this more important, prioritized kind is brought so that he may bless over it first — rather, he blesses over what is before him. Likewise, even if both are before him but he does not wish to eat from both, only from one particular kind, he blesses over the kind he wishes to eat.

clarification.explanation: All the laws of precedence apply only when both kinds are before him and he wishes to eat from both; if one of them is not before him, one does not wait but blesses over what is available. Likewise, if he wishes to eat only from one kind, he blesses over that one alone.
takeaways: The laws of precedence apply only when both kinds are present and he wishes to eat from both.

paragraphs: Even if a fruit of the five kinds that are of the seven species is a half fruit, and the other tree fruits before him are whole, he gives precedence to the fruit of the seven species. But if both are of the seven species, or both are not of the seven species, he gives precedence to the whole one. Likewise, if the ground produce is a whole fruit and the tree fruit is a half fruit, he gives precedence to "borei peri ha'etz." And the same law applies among ground produce itself — he gives precedence to the whole one. And I wrote in the holy book Makbetziel that the requirement to bless over the whole fruit applies only that it be whole at the time of the blessing; but after he has blessed over it, he need not leave it whole in his mouth as it naturally is, since the halachic authorities wrote that one must be careful not to eat a whole fruit as it naturally is, even a single legume, because some say that since it is a whole entity it is called "an important thing" and one blesses an after-blessing over it. And although many disagree with this, and in a case of doubt regarding blessings one is lenient and does not recite an after-blessing over this — nevertheless, why should one eat a whole thing and enter, from the outset, into the very area of the dispute? Therefore he should bless while the fruit is whole, and not put the whole thing into his mouth, but put in part of it and eat part of it, and afterward put in the rest of the fruit; but he should not cut the fruit with his hand after the blessing, because this constitutes a pause between the blessing and the eating. Rather, he should do as we have written: put the fruit into his mouth immediately after the blessing, but not put it all in, only part of it, and bite off part of it with his teeth and eat that part, and then put in the remainder and eat it. And this law applies always, both regarding fruits of the seven species, whose after-blessing is "me'ein shalosh," and regarding other tree fruits, whose after-blessing is "borei nefashot rabot." See Olat Tamid, Eliyah Rabbah, Erech HaShulchan, Chayei Adam, and other later authorities. And this entire caution that we have been warned about, not to eat a whole fruit as it naturally is, applies only if he is not eating from it the measure required for an after-blessing; but if he is eating the measure required for an after-blessing, he may eat it whole, since in any case he is eating a full measure and will recite an after-blessing. Likewise, if he eats these fruits in the course of a meal, after which he will recite Birkat HaMazon, he may eat them whole even if he eats only a single fruit. And know that in our city there are found small dried red grapes called "kishmish" (raisins, not with pits) — with these it is impossible to make the correction we wrote above of putting part of them into his mouth, because they are extremely small; therefore, if he is not eating from them the measure required for an after-blessing, he should withdraw his hand from them and not eat a small amount, for by doing so he enters into the aforementioned dispute regarding the after-blessing, and so too for anything similar to this.

clarification.explanation:
Order of precedence in blessing: even if a fruit of the five kinds (of the seven species) is a half fruit and the other tree fruits before him are whole, he gives precedence to the species of the seven; but if both are of the seven species or both are not, he gives precedence to the whole one. Likewise, if the ground produce is whole and the tree fruit is halved, he gives precedence to "borei peri ha'etz"; and likewise among ground produce itself he gives precedence to the whole one.
And the Ben Ish Chai wrote (in Makbetziel) that the need to bless over the whole applies only at the time of the blessing; but after he has blessed, he should not put the whole fruit into his mouth as it is, because the halachic authorities wrote to be careful not to eat a whole fruit as it naturally is (even a single legume), since some say that a whole entity is considered "an important thing" and one recites an after-blessing over it; and although many disagree and in a doubt regarding blessings one is lenient (and does not recite an after-blessing) — why should one enter, from the outset, into the dispute? Therefore he should bless while the fruit is whole, and then not put the whole thing into his mouth but only part of it, bite off part with his teeth and eat it, and then put in the remainder — and he should not cut it with his hand after the blessing (because of the pause between blessing and eating). This law always applies, both for fruits of the seven species and for others. And this whole caution applies only when he is not eating the measure required for an after-blessing; but if he eats the full measure — he may eat it whole (since he will recite an after-blessing anyway), and likewise if he eats it in the course of a meal. And with small dried raisins, which cannot be divided into parts — if he is not eating the required measure, he should withdraw his hand and not eat from them at all.
takeaways: One gives precedence in blessing to the species of the seven, and among equals — to the whole fruit.

One should not eat a whole fruit as it naturally is (concern of "an important thing") — one blesses while it is whole, puts in part, and bites with the teeth; unless he is eating the full measure required for an after-blessing, or eating it during a meal.
Small raisins that cannot be halved — if there is no full measure, one should not eat from them at all.

paragraphs: Over something that does not grow from the ground, such as meat, fish, eggs, milk, and cheese, one blesses "shehakol," and over truffles one blesses "shehakol."

clarification.explanation: Over things that do not grow from the ground (meat, fish, eggs, milk, cheese) one blesses "shehakol"; and likewise over truffles.
takeaways: Products of animal origin (meat, eggs, milk, cheese) — their blessing is "shehakol."

paragraphs: Fruits of wild trees that are not planted by human hands — one blesses "borei peri ha'etz"; and the same law applies to wild field herbs that are not planted by man — one blesses "borei peri ha'adamah." So is the opinion of our teacher the Ari, of blessed memory, and so is the essential ruling — and not like the halachic authorities who hold that over both of these one blesses "shehakol."

clarification.explanation: Fruits of wild trees not planted by human hand — one blesses "borei peri ha'etz"; and likewise wild field herbs not planted — "borei peri ha'adamah" (following the opinion of the Ari, and not the opinion of those who hold that both are "shehakol").
takeaways: Wild plants (tree/ground) not planted by human hand — one blesses according to their kind (tree/ground), not "shehakol."

paragraphs: Strong vinegar that bubbles when poured onto the ground — one does not bless anything over it, because it causes him harm; but if it is not so strong, he certainly derives benefit from it and blesses "shehakol" over it.

clarification.explanation: Strong vinegar that bubbles when poured onto the ground — one does not bless over it (because it is harmful); weaker vinegar, from which one derives benefit, is blessed "shehakol."
takeaways: Strong, harmful vinegar — no blessing; weak vinegar that one enjoys — "shehakol."

paragraphs: Wine that people refrain from drinking because of its sourness — one does not bless "borei peri hagafen" over it, but rather "shehakol"; and if he erred and blessed "borei peri hagafen," he has fulfilled his obligation.

clarification.explanation: Wine that people avoid drinking because of its sourness — one blesses "shehakol" and not "borei peri hagafen"; if he erred and blessed "hagafen," he has fulfilled his obligation.
takeaways: Overly sour wine — "shehakol" (not "borei peri hagafen"), but after the fact one who blessed "hagafen" has still fulfilled his obligation.

paragraphs: Syrup, which is grape juice that has been concentrated, called in Arabic "dubs" (grape honey) — one blesses over it "shehakol," and after it "borei nefashot rabot." See the later authorities.

clarification.explanation: Concentrated grape-juice syrup (grape honey) — one blesses "shehakol" over it, and "borei nefashot rabot" after it.
takeaways: Grape honey (concentrated syrup) — "shehakol" before it, "borei nefashot rabot" after it.

paragraphs: Sour lemons, and likewise the kind called in Arabic "naranj" (a small, sour citrus fruit): if they are not very sour and are eaten under pressing need, one blesses "shehakol"; but if they are so sour that there is no way to eat them even under pressing need, one does not bless over them. Likewise unripe grapes, called in Arabic "khusrum": if they are not very sour and are eaten under pressing need, one blesses "shehakol" because of the dispute; but if they are very sour and are not eaten even under pressing need, one does not bless over them because they are harmful. See the book Sefer HaLikkutim by our teacher, of blessed memory, in Parashat Ekev, page 107, column 4, and examine it there.

clarification.explanation: Sour citrus fruits (lemon, naranj): if their sourness is moderate and they are eaten under pressing need — "shehakol"; if they are too sour to eat even under pressing need — one does not bless over them. Likewise unripe grapes.
takeaways: Very sour fruits (lemon, unripe grapes) that are eaten only under pressing need — "shehakol"; those too sour to eat at all — no blessing.

paragraphs: One who drinks water for his thirst blesses "shehakol" and afterward "borei nefashot rabot"; but if he was not eager to drink, but rather a piece of food was choking him and he drank water to clear that piece, he does not bless either before or after, since he derives no benefit from it. The same law applies if he drinks water in order to swallow a medicine, since he is not eager for the water, he should not bless, and so too in similar cases. But if he drank another beverage to clear the choking piece and the like, he does bless over the beverage, since he does derive benefit from it.

clarification.explanation: One who drinks water for his thirst — "shehakol" and afterward "borei nefashot rabot"; but if he drinks only to clear something stuck in his throat (without thirst) — he does not bless at all, since he derives no benefit. Likewise one who drinks water to swallow medicine. But if he drinks another beverage (not water) for the same purpose, he does bless, since he derives benefit from it.
takeaways: Water without real thirst (only to clear stuck food/medicine) — no blessing at all; another beverage for the same purpose — one does bless (there is benefit).

paragraphs: All foods and drinks that a person eats and drinks for medicinal purposes — if their taste is good and the palate enjoys them, he blesses over them both before and after; but if he was forced to eat or drink them, even though the palate enjoys them, he does not bless over them, since he was compelled to do so.

clarification.explanation: Foods and drinks eaten or drunk for medicinal purposes — if their taste is good and the palate enjoys them, one blesses before and after them; but if he was forced to eat them (compelled) — he does not bless, even though there is enjoyment.
takeaways: Tasty medicine — one blesses if eaten willingly; if forced under compulsion — one does not bless even if there is enjoyment.

paragraphs: If he forgot and put food into his mouth without a blessing and remembered before chewing it — if it is something that will not become repulsive to him if he spits it out, he spits it into his hands and blesses over it and eats it, and he should not bless while it is still in his mouth, because it is written (Psalms 71:8), "Let my mouth be filled with Your praise" — and how can he bless with his mouth full of food? But if it is something that will become repulsive to him if he spits it out, he moves it to one side of his mouth and blesses over it, because it is forbidden to waste food. But if this happens to him with liquids, which he cannot move to one side, he should spit out these liquids and let them go to waste. And if he is in urgent need of these liquids in his mouth, such that he must swallow them, it seems to me that he should recite the blessing mentally in his heart and swallow them, for we hold that a mental recitation suffices in a case of compulsion, as we have written regarding this elsewhere. But he should not do the correction that Rabbi Shlomo Ganzfried, of blessed memory, wrote in Kitzur Shulchan Aruch, chapter 50, paragraph 10, namely to swallow first and afterward recite the first blessing.

clarification.explanation: If he forgot and put food in his mouth without a blessing and remembered before chewing it: if spitting it out will not be repulsive to him — he spits it into his hands, blesses, and eats it (one may not bless with a full mouth). If spitting it out would be repulsive — he moves it to one side of his mouth and blesses (it is forbidden to waste food). With a liquid that cannot be moved to one side — he spits it out to be wasted; and if he is in such urgent need of the liquid in his mouth that he cannot spit it out, he should recite the blessing mentally in his heart and swallow it, since a mental recitation is effective in a case of compulsion. And the author writes that one should not follow the practice of Rabbi Shlomo Ganzfried in Kitzur Shulchan Aruch (chapter 50, paragraph 10), who wrote to swallow first and only afterward recite the first blessing — rather, one should recite the blessing mentally in the heart before swallowing, as stated.
takeaways: One who forgot to bless and already has food in his mouth — spits it into his hands or moves it to one side and blesses; with an urgent liquid that cannot be spat out — a mental recitation before swallowing suffices.
The author disagrees with the Kitzur Shulchan Aruch's advice to swallow first and bless afterward; the halachah is to recite the blessing mentally in the heart before swallowing, not to bless after.

paragraphs: In the blessing "shehakol nihyah bidvaro" ("by whose word all things came to be") is alluded to the rectification of the mixture of good and evil that came about through the sin of Adam, the first man, for Scripture says (Deuteronomy 8:3), "By everything that proceeds from the mouth of the Lord does man live," for by the word of the mouth of the Lord everything was made in the work of Creation, such that for anything He wished, He would say "let it be so," and it was so — for by the power of the speech of the Holy One, blessed be He, all creatures came into being, and this is called "that which proceeds from the mouth of the Lord." And by all of His speech, blessed be He, man, animal, plant, and mineral live, for the spirituality of that utterance became clothed within every single thing. And this is why they instituted in the blessing over enjoyment "shehakol nihyah bidvaro," for this is an all-encompassing blessing, since we hold (Berachot 40a): over anything, if one said "shehakol," he has fulfilled his obligation. Therefore, by the power of this blessing, all the spirituality and holiness ascends above to its place and is rectified from the damage it suffered from the sin of Adam, the first man — all of this is mentioned in the words of our teacher, of blessed memory, in Sefer HaLikkutim, printed in the holy city of Jerusalem, may it be rebuilt and reestablished speedily, in Parashat Ekev; examine it there.

clarification.explanation: In the blessing "shehakol nihyah bidvaro" is alluded to the rectification of the mixture of good and evil that came about through the sin of Adam, the first man: all of creation was made by "the word of the mouth of the Lord" ("let it be so, and it was so"), and the spirituality of that speech becomes clothed within every single thing. The blessing of "shehakol" (a general blessing which fulfills one's obligation for everything) raises up that same spirituality and holiness to its place above, and rectifies the damage caused to it by the sin of Adam, the first man.
takeaways: The blessing "shehakol" raises up and rectifies the spirituality within food, which was damaged by the sin of Adam, the first man — because it is a general blessing that applies to everything.

paragraphs: In the after-blessing, which is the blessing "borei nefashot rabot" ("who creates many souls"), is alluded to the rectification of souls reincarnated in plants or animals or other kinds, which are reincarnated there because of their sin, and are rectified and ascend from there by the power of the blessing. And this is its explanation: "Blessed are You, Lord our God, King of the universe, who creates many souls" — from among His creatures, "and their lacks, for all that You have created" — meaning, because of their lack they must be reincarnated into one of these kinds, each one according to its sin, and therefore we need, by the power of this blessing, "to give life through them to the soul of every living thing" that is reincarnated there, and therefore "Blessed is He, the life of the worlds," who performs so great a wonder as this through us.

clarification.explanation: In the after-blessing "borei nefashot rabot" is alluded to the rectification of souls reincarnated in plants, animals, or other kinds because of their sins — and they are rectified and ascend by the power of the blessing. The meaning of the blessing: God "creates many souls" from among His creatures, and "their lacks, for all that You have created" (meaning, because of their lack they must be reincarnated, each according to its sin) — and therefore "He gives life through them to the soul of every living thing" reincarnated there, and therefore "Blessed is He, the life of the worlds."
takeaways: The blessing "borei nefashot rabot" helps rectify souls reincarnated within creation (plant/animal) because of their sins.
